The v3.0 results state Clang 21, C++23, 'Linux x86_64, 32 cores, 2995 MHz', but give no CPU model and no flags for that run (only the legacy section says -O3). That falls short of A, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No valid win over simdjson. Parse: simdjson is 46x-116x faster (small 162B: 1,495 ns vs 33 ns; medium 12KB: 113 us vs 1.1 us; large 1MB: 23.2 ms vs 201 us; 83-112 MB/s vs 4.1-11.1 GB/s). The page's two 'wins' are field access (52 ns vs 66 ns, 1.26x) and array iteration over 10K records (198 us vs 444 us, 2.24x). In the source, FastJSON's DOM is built once outside the timed loop, while simdjson's loop includes parser.iterate() plus its lazy parse. Adding FastJSON's own parse times from the same page gives ~1,547 ns vs 66 ns (~23x slower) and ~23.4 ms vs 444 us (~53x slower) (derived from page data). The 7.8x ondemand figure (2.97 ms vs 23.2 ms) compares FastJSON against itself. The page's legacy Nov 2025 section, 'FJITW 9-16% faster parse, 1.8-7.6x faster filter than simdjson', came from benchmarks/comparative_benchmark.cpp, whose 'simdjson' is a SimdJsonSimulator class that calls std::this_thread::sleep_for. It is not simdjson.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Clang 21, C++23, Google Benchmark (v3.0 run; optimization flags not stated for this run; legacy Nov 2025 section says Clang 21.1.5 -O3)
corrections.caveats: The only numbers against real simdjson show it 46x-116x slower on parse. The two 'wins' (field access 1.26x, array iteration 2.24x) come from an asymmetric harness in benchmarks/fastjson_vs_simdjson.cpp: FastJSON is parsed once outside the timed loop, while simdjson ondemand's parser.iterate() plus parse runs inside it. Counting FastJSON's own parse times from the page, simdjson wins both, by ~23x and ~53x (derived). The simdjson 'parse' rows time only ondemand parser.iterate(), which is structural indexing without value materialization, so the raw-parse ratio is not like-for-like either. The page's legacy Nov 2025 'faster than simdjson' tables are invalid: benchmarks/comparative_benchmark.cpp uses a SimdJsonSimulator built on sleep_for, not simdjson. License: LICENSE_BSD_4_CLAUSE is the original 4-clause BSD with an advertising clause (the README confirms it). That license is not OSI-approved and is GPL-incompatible, and GitHub reports it as NOASSERTION. Solo project, 0 stars, sprawling repo (Bazel, ai/, python bindings, many top-level docs) consistent with heavy AI-assisted authoring. No independent reproduction. No CPU model stated.

corrections.caveats: Self-described learning project, solo author, 0 stars. The repo dates from 2021; the benchmarks and the vector-based containers behind the read win were added 2026-09-22. No CPU model, compiler or flags are stated for the numbers. The results table is in the root README, and the methodology and usability annex are in the Spanish benchmarks/README.md, which has no numbers. It loses on write: nlohmann/json is faster at every size (34.0 vs 21.0 us, 4,388.1 vs 3,042.3 us, 32,568.2 vs 21,225.0 us). It also loses to RapidJSON, simdjson (DOM) and glaze json_t on both read and write. The author says he would pick glaze for real use and praises RapidJSON. The win over nlohmann/json (1.25x-1.42x read) is modest. The README documents that libJSON has no public API for modifying an existing field. Unlicense public-domain dedication, so there is no patent grant.
